Five Minds, One Mission!
summary:
Nexus-V is a web game for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Space Mission Design Game”. Players plan, build and launch a space mission, then learn why it succeeded or failed. Teammates join a shared live lobby through an invite link, then work through the mission together.
In the Plan stage, players set a budget, choose a planet and pick a mission type: flyby, orbit, landing, or orbit and return. In the Build stage they choose a launch vehicle, payload, power system, antenna and propulsion stage, while live limit bars for mass, power, delta-v, comms and budget show when a limit is broken. These limits come from real physics, including the rocket equation and solar power falling with distance from the Sun. During launch, anomalies such as solar flares and thruster failures force decisions. A final score out of 1,000 and a plain-language debrief explain what worked and what didn’t.
Nexus-V makes space mission engineering approachable and teaches real trade-offs by playing. It is built with React, Vite, TypeScript and Express, using data from real missions such as Perseverance, Juno and Cassini.
details:
Nexus-V is a web game, built by Team Nexus V, where a team plans, builds and launches a space mission, then learns why it succeeded or failed. Players set a budget, choose a planet and pick a mission type (flyby, orbit, landing, or orbit and return). They then build a spacecraft from a launch vehicle, payload, power system, antenna and propulsion stage. Live limit bars for mass, power, delta-v, comms and budget show when a limit is broken, and Launch stays locked until nothing is over its limit. During flight, anomalies such as solar storms and thruster failures force a decision, and each choice has costs and consequences. A final score out of 1,000 and a plain-language debrief explain what worked and what didn’t.

Teamwork
A team creates a lobby, shares an invite link, and up to four players join it live. The idea is to make collaboration and communication the core of the game, as in real missions.

Benefits and impact
Players learn real mission trade-offs by playing: heavier payloads need bigger rockets, solar power fades with distance from the Sun, and far targets need nuclear power and stronger antennas. The debrief names the cause of every failure and suggests a fix, so players learn from each run and can try again.

Tools and technology
React , Vite , TypeScript , Tailwind CSS and React Router for the frontend, and Node.js with Express for the multiplayer lobby, deployed on Vercel. The physics is custom TypeScript: the rocket equation for delta-v, orbital transfer figures, solar power falling with distance squared, and light-time communication delay.

Creativity
The retro “cyber-cockpit” interface gives the game a mission-control feel. Parts and planets are modeled on real missions, including Perseverance, Juno, Cassini and Voyager 2. Estimated prices are marked with a tilde (~) so players know which figures are sourced.

What we considered
We balanced realism with beginner-friendliness, keeping the physics accurate but the explanations simple. Next steps include shared mission state and team voting during flight events.
